newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Canberra pressed on foreign media ownership limits.
newsitem.headline: Canberra pressed on foreign media ownership limits.

text.p: The Australian government faced mounting pressure on Tuesday to ease limits on foreign ownership of newspapers and television, as the country's competition watchdog backed media owners in urging more liberal media laws.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission said in its submission to a government media ownership review that tight limits on foreign holdings shielded the domestic media from international competition and limited diversity.
"We, in our submission, suggest that the present (foreign ownership) restrictions are much too restrictive," Commission chairman Allan Fels said in a radio interview on Tuesday.
"We may need a more flexible approach than rigid rules about the degree of foreign ownership such as we have at the present time," Fels said.
Media laws currently limit foreign ownership to 25 percent in newspapers and 15 percent in television companies.

Canadian media proprietor Conrad Black has threatened to offload his 25 percent stake in John Fairfax Holdings Ltd, Australia's oldest media group, if Australia does not ease what he called "anachronistic" foreign ownership limits.
Black said last week he wanted to lift his stake in Fairfax, which publishes The Sydney Morning Herald, The Age and The Australian Financial Review newspapers, to 50 percent.
Prime Minister John Howard's Liberal-National government, elected in March, has ordered a review of media laws which limit cross ownership of newspapers and television stations.
The limits bar a newspaper proprietor owning more than 15 percent of a television station in the same city and vice-versa for owners of television stations.
But the review is not examining foreign ownership rules.
Howard, responding to Fels in a separate radio interview, said there was already a strong view in the community that existing foreign holdings were high.

News Ltd, the Australian unit of Rupert Murdoch's global media group News Corp, issued a statement saying it was urging the government to ease all media ownership restrictions. Although born in Australia, Murdoch is now a U.S. citizen.

"Our submission (to the inquiry) encourages liberalising all regulations restricting ownership of the media market in order to increase competition and diversity of opinion, thereby better serving the interests of consumers," News Ltd executive chairman Ken Cowley said in a statement.
News Corp publishes the national daily, The Australian, and most of the major daily city newspapers.

"It has been our long-held view that regulatory intervention in the industry is counter-productive to its efficient growth, to encouraging competition and circulation of the widest possible spread of information and opinions through the community," Cowley said.
"They straitjacket the Australian media and prohibit it from fully delivering to consumers the benefits of active participation in the global ideas marketplace."

Media concern Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd (PBL), controlled by Australia's richest man Kerry Packer, is against any relaxation of the foreign ownership limit that would allow foreign investors to boost their Australia media holdings. PBL is a major television broadcaster and magazine publisher that also holds a 15 percent stake in Fairfax.
The media review is expected to be completed in early 1997.
